chunks: And by this chain, he this chain, he said,

I said to Abu Ibrahim (peace be upon him), 'If a man mortgages a slave and a house, and the affliction (loss of value) hits it, upon whom would that be?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Upon his master.' Then he (peace be upon him) said: 'What is your view if he kills a person (diyya is paid), upon whom would that be?' I said, 'It is in the neck of the slave.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Do you not see that his wealth has not gone away?' Then he (peace be upon him) said: 'What is your view if his price was one hundred Dinars, so it increased and reached two hundred Dinars, for whom would that be?' I said, 'For his master.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Like that is what would be against him, what would be for him.'

key_terms.عُنُقِ الْعَبْدِ: In the neck of the slave (liability attached to him)
key_terms.قَتِيلًا: A slain person (liability for blood money)

ai.seo_question: Who bears the financial liability and benefits from the appreciation of a mortgaged slave or property in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) elucidates the principle of 'liability follows ownership' (al-ghurm bi al-ghunm) by using the analogy of a slave's blood money, demonstrating that the master bears the financial burden while retaining the asset's value appreciation. This ruling establishes that in a mortgage (rahn), the debtor retains the risk of loss and the benefit of increase, ensuring that the creditor's claim is limited to the debt amount without encroaching on the debtor's broader wealth. This hadith serves as a foundational juristic proof for the equitable distribution of risk and reward in Islamic financial transactions.

en.hubeali: ‘I said to Abu Ibrahim<sup>asws</sup> (7<sup>th</sup> Imam<sup>asws</sup>), ‘The man mortgages the slave and the house, so the affliction hits it, upon whom would that (loss) happen to be?’ He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘Upon his master’. Then he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘What is your view if people are killed, upon who would that be?’ I said, ‘It would be in the neck of the slave’. He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘Do you not see that his wealth has not gone away?’ Then he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘What is your view if his price was one hundred Dinars, so it increased and reached two hundred Dinars, for whom would that have been?’ I said, ‘For his master’. He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘Like that is what would happen to be against him, what would happen to be for him’.
en.sarwar: 10. Through the same chain of narrators as that of the previous Hadith the following is narrated: “

I once asked abu Ibrahim, Alayhi al-Salam, about the case of a man who mortgaged a slave and the house and they suffered loss; if it was compensated by a particular party. He (the Imam) said, ‘His master is responsible.’ He (the Imam) then said, ‘Suppose if someone is murdered who is responsible?’ I replied, ‘It is on the neck of the slave.’ He (the Imam) said, ‘Do you not consider that his property is not gone?’ He (the Imam) then said, ‘Consider, if his price was one hundred dinar and it increased up to two hundred dinars. To whom does it (the increase) belong?’ I replied, ‘It belongs to his master.’ He (the Imam) said, ‘In the same way it is on him just as it is for him.’”
